title: Let a provisioner create contexts beneath its own without administrat…
body:
…ive authority: the additive context-create capability (VTI-CTX-026 – VTI-CTX-028)

A process that mints a context for each software agent it manages sits on a host that faces the network, so it should not hold the administrative role: an administrator of a context can write access control entries for it, and a compromise of the process would then rewrite everything it created. Creating a context is the one power it needs.

VTI-CTX-020 already requires act authority covering the parent, and VTI-ACL-033 already defines an additive capability, so this adds no new mechanism. It registers one capability and states what it confers:

- VTI-CTX-026: an entry holding `context-create` may create a context beneath one its act scope covers, whatever its role, meeting the same creation requirements as any other creator.
- VTI-CTX-027: it never permits a root context or one outside the entry's act scope, confers nothing else, and writes no access control entry for the creator, so authority cannot accumulate one context at a time. Consistent with VTI-VTA-032.
- VTI-CTX-028: it may name a covered context's primary DID, only while that context has none and only to an identifier the context's own keys control; changing or clearing it stays an administrator's act. A context with no identity can be issued as nothing, so without this a creator would need an administrator to finish every context it makes.

Appendix C.2 gains the `context-create` row and the reason it is additive.

The alternative considered, a separate always-available service holding unrestricted act authority that creates contexts on callers' behalf, is recorded in the rationale and rejected: it is a new component whose only purpose is to hold the most powerful grant in the system.

This is a change proposal against the requirements. It is deliberately not a divergence-register entry, and records nothing about any implementation.
author: DenisPopov15
significance_reasons: Authority, delegation, approval, or revocation semantics

Release notes

Sourced from dart-lang/setup-dart's releases.

v1.8.2

  • Update publish.yml to a three-job workflow (validate, package, publish) supporting hermetic package archiving (--to-archive / --from-archive).
  • Add sdk input to publish.yml to support publishing packages that require a non-stable Dart SDK (e.g., beta or dev).
  • Fix registering the dart analyze problem matcher when setup-dart runs as a step of a composite action (#198[]).
  • Bump undici to 6.29.0 and @vercel/ncc to 0.45.0.

#198: dart-lang/setup-dart#198

Changelog

Sourced from dart-lang/setup-dart's changelog.

v1.8.2

  • Update publish.yml to a three-job workflow (validate, package, publish) supporting hermetic package archiving (--to-archive / --from-archive).
  • Add sdk input to publish.yml to support publishing packages that require a non-stable Dart SDK (e.g., beta or dev).
  • Fix registering the dart analyze problem matcher when setup-dart runs as a step of a composite action (#198[]).
  • Bump undici to 6.29.0 and @vercel/ncc to 0.45.0.

#198: dart-lang/setup-dart#198

v1.8.1

  • Update workflows to pin actions/checkout to a commit SHA.
  • Harden workflow permissions to contents: read.
  • Update publish.yml reusable workflow to reference setup-dart@v1.8.0 and latest setup-flutter.
  • Bump undici to 6.28.0 and @vercel/ncc to 0.44.1.

v1.8.0

  • Add a problem matcher for dart analyze to automatically create inline annotations on GitHub pull requests.
  • Update publish.yml reusable workflow to reference setup-dart@v1.7.2 (running on Node 24) (#188[]).
  • Update GitHub Action dependencies (actions/checkout v7).
  • Bump undici to 6.27.0 and update npm dependencies.

#188: dart-lang/setup-dart#188

v1.7.2

  • Update Node.js requirement to Node 24.
  • Fix open Dependabot alerts by bumping undici to >=6.24.0.
  • Update GitHub Action dependencies (@actions/core, @actions/exec, @actions/tool-cache, @actions/http-client).
  • Update workflow actions to their latest versions (actions/checkout v6, setup-flutter).

v1.7.1

  • Roll undici dependency to address CVE-2025-22150.
  • Update to the latest npm dependencies.
  • Recompile the action using the new Dart / JavaScript interop.

v1.7.0

  • Install flutter sdk in publishing step, allowing Flutter packages to be published (#68[])

    #68: dart-lang/setup-dart#68

title: feat(vtc): a community room's signal delay is chosen at creation and changed on its page (create 0.5, update 0.4, get 0.5)
body:
Implements trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#1336.

**Draft: waits for #1336 to merge.** `vti-specs-vtc` is pinned from a local build of that branch, so `trust-tasks.lock` currently records a `file://` registry. Once #1336 is published, re-pin from trusttasks.org; the bundles are deterministic, so the digests should not change.

## Why
A room the community owns was always created with the randomised watch-signal delay, and nothing could change it.
- `vtc/rooms/community/create` and `update` had no `signalDelay`.
- `rooms/signal-delay/set` is sent to a room's host by a holder of its `admin`, and for a community room both of those are the community itself.

So the console had nothing to offer.

## What changes
- **vtc-service** serves create 0.5, update 0.4 and get 0.5 beside the older versions (create 0.4, update 0.3, get 0.3/0.4).
  - The delay is stored in the room's host record (`vti_rooms::Room::signal_delay`), which the watcher reads each time it fires.
  - Update writes the host record first, then the owner's record, and puts the host record back if the owner's write fails.
  - Changing only the delay counts as a `detailsUpdated` change, audited with the old and new values. It needs no profile write.
  - A create with `none` is audited along with the create.
  - The community accepts either setting, so `signalDelayNotPermitted` can't be emitted. It is listed in the error-code census baseline.
- **Console**
  - **New community room** and **Edit details** get a *Watch signals* choice: after a short random wait (the default) or at once. Choosing *at once* shows what it gives up before anything is sent.
  - The room's page shows the current setting.
  - The host's page for a community-owned room now points to Community rooms instead of `pnm`.
- **cnm**: `rooms create|update --signal-delay randomised|none`, with the same warning before it sends `none`.
- **vtc-mcp**: `room_open` creates at 0.5.
- **vta-sdk**: OpenAPI wrappers for the three new versions. The old wrappers are kept, since removing one is a breaking change.
- **Docs**: `community-rooms.md` has a new *Watch signals* section; `data-rooms.md` is updated.

## Tests
- `cargo nextest run --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client`: 7701 passed.
- `cargo nextest run -p vtc-service -p vtc-client`: everything passed except 7 tests on the first run.
  - 6 of them check the embedded admin-UI bundle and fail whenever the run uses `VTC_SKIP_ADMIN_UI_BUILD=1`.
  - The 7th was a real omission (`get/0.5` missing from the proof-requirement allowlist), now fixed.
  - All 7 pass on a re-run with the UI built.
- Doctests, `clippy -D warnings`, `fmt --check` and `check-docs.py` pass.
- Console: `npm run lint`; vitest for the plugins passes 640 tests, then 58 in the two rooms files after the new tests were added.
- New tests:
  - Integration test `vtc_rooms_community_signal_delay_is_set_at_create_read_and_changed`.
  - Conformance entries for the three new versions.
  - Console tests for the create toggle, the edit toggle and `detailsUpdate`.
  - A cnm payload test.

title: spec(vtc/rooms/community): a community-owned room states and changes its signal delay (create 0.5, update 0.4, get 0.5)
body:
A room a member owns states its signal delay at `rooms/create` 0.3, and its administrators change it at the host with `rooms/signal-delay/set` 0.1 (#1084). A room the **community** owns could do neither. The community is both the holder of `admin` and the host, and `vtc/rooms/community/create` and `update` had no field for it, so every community room waited a randomised few seconds before each `rooms/changed` signal, however its members used it. As a result, the VTC console can't offer the setting.

## What this adds
- **`vtc/rooms/community/create/0.5`**: an optional `signalDelay` (absent means `randomised`). It is recorded in the room's host record and always echoed back. A `none` create is audited along with the create.
- **`vtc/rooms/community/update/0.4`**: an optional `signalDelay`, applied together with the other details or not at all.
  - Changing only the delay counts as a change: it is audited, and `detailsUpdatedAt` and `detailsUpdatedBy` move. It needs no profile write.
  - It touches no watch.
  - Updating the host record is now allowed for this one field.
- **`vtc/rooms/community/get/0.5`**: always returns the room's `signalDelay`.
- **Refusal on both writes:** `signalDelayNotPermitted` when the community's governance as host keeps the delay for every room. Nothing in the request is applied.
- **Surfaces:** a surface that offers `none` SHOULD say what it gives up.

Links to create 0.4, update 0.3 and get 0.4 have moved to the new versions (`npm run fix-stale-references`).

## Checks run
- Rust, TS, Go and Dart libraries regenerated.
- Passed: `npm run check`, `check-bindings`, `build`, `build-bundles` + `check-bundles`, and the `trust-tasks-rs` conformance tests (4104 passed).

Consumer: VTI (the VTC console's create form gets the setting, and a community room's page can edit it).

title: fix(vtc): a member can add a passkey with a hardware key when their DID is long
body:
Hi Glenn,

Thanks for all the work on VTI. I ran into a bug while adding a passkey in the member portal, and this started as my attempt at a small fix. It now includes your follow-up commits (a708b13ba, 55327b668).

## The problem

On the member portal, adding a passkey with a YubiKey failed with "Passkey creation was cancelled". The PIN was accepted, but the touch prompt never appeared. The same key worked on other VTCs.

The cause is the name we send to the authenticator. `register_start` passes the member's whole DID as WebAuthn `user.name` and `user.displayName`. A `did:webvh` is about 95 bytes, and this key rejects a `user.name` longer than 64 bytes. CTAP2 only requires authenticators to accept 64. The key answers `CTAP1_ERR_INVALID_LENGTH` before asking for a touch, and Chrome turns any such CTAP error into a generic `NotAllowedError`, which is where the "cancelled" message comes from.

## How I checked

I took the exact options the portal returns and ran them against the key directly (python-fido2) and through `navigator.credentials.create` in Chrome. Only the name changed between runs:

| `user.name` | CTAP result | Chrome |
|---|---|---|
| 95 bytes (the DID) | `INVALID_LENGTH` (0x03), no touch prompt | `NotAllowedError` |
| 64 bytes | OK | not run |
| 65 bytes | `INVALID_LENGTH` | not run |
| 59 bytes (output of the original version of this PR) | OK | OK |

A long `displayName` on its own was accepted; only `user.name` is limited. PIN, `credProtect`, `userVerification: required` and the algorithm list were identical in every run.

Environment: YubiKey 5 series, firmware 5.7.4, Chrome 156 on Linux. I only tried this one key, so other keys may behave differently.

## The change (current head)

- `vti_common::auth::passkey::AuthenticatorName` is the only way to build a name for an authenticator (`for_did`, `from_label`, `for_did_or_label`), and it is bounded to 64 **bytes**. `vti_common::auth::passkey::start_passkey_registration` is the one place a registration starts. The VTC wrapper, the three VTC DID-named paths (member portal, admin passkeys, step-up redeem), the VTC install ceremony and the VTA passkey-VM enrolment all go through it.
- Naming rules:
  - `did:webvh` / `did:tdw`: `<host:path> (<last 6 chars of SCID>)`, e.g. `dids.example.org:example-member-000001 (000000)`. If host+path doesn't fit it keeps both ends joined by `…`.
  - Any other DID: unchanged if 64 bytes or less, otherwise first 40 bytes + `…` + last 21 bytes.
  - VTA operator-supplied label: used as given; if over 64 bytes, `…` plus its tail.
  - All cuts are on char boundaries. The same name is applied to `user.name` and `user.displayName`.
- The VTA's old `display_name_for` is removed. It capped at 64 characters, not bytes, and its long branch produced 66 bytes, so it had the same bug.
- The private copy of `authenticator_name` in `step_up_passkey.rs` is removed.

The name is display only. The account is still identified by `user.id` and this service's own record, as before.

Behaviour changes to be aware of: a webvh name now carries a SCID fragment and shows host+path rather than the first-40/last-16 form, so names differ from what the step-up flow showed before, and from what the VTA produced.

## Testing

- CI is green on the current head.
- Glenn reports vtc-service + vtc-client 3598/3598, vti-common and vta-service passkey tests, workspace clippy `-D warnings` and doc tests all passing locally.
- YubiKey check on the current head (55327b668): I ran a local test VTC built from this head and added a passkey from Chrome with the same YubiKey. It worked: the touch prompt appeared and the passkey registered. The server returned `user.name` and `user.displayName` of `first.example.com:members:alice (2bwPSE)` (40 bytes) for an 88-byte `did:webvh`, where the original code sent all 88. This used the repo's `TestVtc` harness with a wallet-proven member session, not the real wallet sign-in, and not a deployed community portal.
- I have **not** run it against a deployed portal such as the one where I first hit the bug; that is still open.
- Test gaps I'd like covered (also requested in my comment above): `did:webvh:<scid>:` with an empty tail and `did:webvh:<scid>` with no colon; host+path of exactly 64 and 65 bytes; exact-output assertions for 2-byte and 3-byte characters; and one test that the options returned by the three DID-named call sites carry the short name.

## Open questions

- Over-length webvh with a long host: the host head is capped at about 26 bytes, so hosts longer than that are cut inside the host. Is that acceptable?
- An over-long VTA `label` keeps its tail; for free text, keeping the head may read better.

Thanks for taking a look.

Brendan

Adding a passkey in the member portal failed on a YubiKey 5 (firmware
5.7.4) with "Passkey creation was cancelled": the key answered
CTAP1_ERR_INVALID_LENGTH to the registration, after the PIN and before
any touch prompt, and Chrome reports every such CTAP error as a generic
NotAllowedError.

The portal sent the member's whole DID as WebAuthn user.name and
user.displayName. A did:webvh is ~95 bytes, and the key rejects a
user.name over 64 bytes (CTAP2 only requires authenticators to accept
64). Tried against the key, with only the name changed: 64 bytes passes,
65 fails, and a long displayName on its own is accepted.

The step-up enrolment flow already shortened a long DID to its two ends
(authenticator_name), but the member portal and the admin passkey paths
call start_passkey_registration directly and did not. Move that helper
into the shared start_passkey_registration wrapper so every registration
shows the same short name, count it in bytes rather than characters so a
multi-byte DID cannot pass 64 bytes, and drop the private copy in
step_up_passkey.

The name is display only; the account is identified by user.id and this
service's own record, as before. A DID of 64 bytes or less is unchanged.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Brendan A. Miller <code+os@brendanmiller.com>

* fix(passkey): one byte-bounded authenticator name for the VTA and the VTC

The VTA's passkey-VM enrolment had the same defect this PR fixes in the
VTC: `display_name_for` capped the name at 64 characters, not bytes, and
its long branch emitted `…` plus 63 characters, 66 bytes even for ASCII,
so a YubiKey 5 refuses `vta/passkey-vms/*` enrolment for a long webvh
path or operator label. The two services kept separate copies of the
rule, which is how they drifted.

Move the rule to `vti_common::auth::passkey`, beside `build_webauthn`:
`MAX_AUTHENTICATOR_NAME_BYTES`, `authenticator_name_for_did` and
`clamp_authenticator_name`. A did:webvh is named by its host and path
(its SCID is unreadable and the head of the DID is almost all SCID);
other long DIDs keep their two ends. The VTC wrapper now only enforces
the byte limit, and its DID-named callers pass
`authenticator_name_for_did`.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* refactor(passkey): one AuthenticatorName type and one registration start for the VTA and the VTC

Review follow-up on the byte-bounded authenticator name.

- `vti_common::auth::passkey::AuthenticatorName` replaces the free
  `authenticator_name_for_did` / `clamp_authenticator_name`. It is only
  built by `for_did`, `from_label` or `for_did_or_label`, so a name over
  64 bytes cannot reach an authenticator, and a caller can no longer pass
  a raw DID by mistake (the test fixtures did, and so exercised naming
  production never used).
- `vti_common::auth::passkey::start_passkey_registration` is the one
  place both services start a registration: the VTA's passkey-VM
  enrolment, the VTC wrapper (which adds EdDSA on top) and the VTC install
  ceremony. The bound is no longer enforced twice in the VTC and separately
  in the VTA.
- `did:tdw` (webvh's earlier name) is named like `did:webvh`, as the VTA's
  old `display_name_for` did for any SCID-first method.
- A webvh name ends with the SCID's last six characters,
  `dids.example.org:persona (wUF4kX)`, so two DIDs re-created at one path
  are told apart in the picker.
- A webvh host and path too long to fit keep both ends, so the host stays
  visible rather than only the path's tail.
- Uses std's `floor_char_boundary` / `ceil_char_boundary` (MSRV 1.95).
- The naming tests live with the type and check every cut is a true head
  and tail of its source, so a split character fails them.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

  • evaluate() reported a missing single required name beside additionalProperties: false at /additionalProperties (it should be /required).

[0.61.1] - 2026-11-10

Added

Fixed

  • . in pattern and patternProperties matched \r, U+2028 and U+2029 (it should reject every line terminator).

  • Building validators up to 25% faster on schemas that declare a base URI, from building absolute keyword locations on first use.
  • Building validators up to 3% faster, from cheaper compilation cache keys.
  • oneOf / anyOf up to 7x faster when branches fix a property with const or enum.
  • oneOf / anyOf skip branches that exclude the instance's value with not over enum or const.
  • properties up to 40% faster on objects with a few more keys than it declares.
  • minLength / maxLength skip counting code points when the byte length decides.
  • pattern starting with lookaheads (^(?=...)(?=...)...) up to 2x faster.
  • properties and additionalProperties up to 13% faster on schemas declaring 15 or more properties.
  • properties up to 12% faster on objects with keys it does not declare.
  • Validation up to 40% faster with serde_json's preserve_order feature.
  • unevaluatedProperties up to 10% faster on schemas that combine it with patternProperties or applicators.
  • required up to 40% faster when it lists every property of an object closed by additionalProperties: false.
  • properties, anyOf and other applicators faster on subschemas that only check a non-numeric type, directly or through $ref.

## `vta-signing`

## [0.1.0](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/releases/tag/vta-signing-v0.1.0) — 2026-11-18 ### Added - **vta-signing**: A small signing library the VTA and its callers share ([#2745](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2745)) * feat(keys): keys/sign-jws/0.1 — a VTA-built compact JWS walled off to JWT types Add a `keys/sign-jws/0.1` Trust Task that produces a compact JWS (a JWT) over a caller-supplied JOSE header and claims set, signed by a stored key. Unlike `keys/sign/0.1` it is not a general signing oracle: the VTA assembles the `b64url(header).b64url(payload)` signing input itself and signs it under `SigningDomain::ProtocolDefined`, so the result verifies as a JWS rather than as a VTA opaque-signing payload. The task is walled off so it can never be pointed at producing a credential or issuer artifact: - the finalized protected header's `typ` must be on a small allow-list of JWT profiles (`JWT`, `at+jwt`, `oauth-id-jag+jwt`, `dpop+jwt`, `logout+jwt`); anything else — e.g. a Verifiable Credential media type — is refused before the key is touched; - the VTA, not the caller, sets `alg` from the key, so a caller cannot request a signature under an algorithm the key does not implement or mislabel one; - the payload must be a JSON object (a JWT claims set); raw bytes still go through the opaque oracle, not here. Authorized exactly as `keys/sign` is — per the key's context — so the same context separation that walls off a signer's identities applies. Added to the dispatch table with the spec's (none / none / actsAsSubject) class, and acknowledged in `UNSPECCED_DISPATCHED_URIS` pending an upstream spec in trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf (dispatched unvalidated like any unknown-schema task until then). Enables the Agent Gateway to delegate JWT signing (STS access tokens, ID-JAG) to the VTA while keeping the JWT-signing path structurally separate from credential signing.
## `vti-specs-vta`
## [0.11.0](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/compare/vti-specs-vta-v0.10.0...vti-specs-vta-v0.11.0) — 2026-11-18 ### Added - **vta**: Every DID the VTA holds through one method-neutral surface (vta/dids/*) ([#2763](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2763)) * feat(vta)!: every DID the VTA holds through one method-neutral surface (vta/dids/*)
## `vti-specs-vtc`
## [0.7.1](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/compare/vti-specs-vtc-v0.7.0...vti-specs-vtc-v0.7.1) — 2026-11-18 ### Added - **vtc-service**: Serve vtc/storage/credentials/recipient/0.1 so the console seals for any DID method ([#2762](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2762)) * feat(vtc-service): serve vtc/storage/credentials/recipient/0.1 so the console seals for any DID method The console sealed a storage credential to the key it read from the community's same-origin /.well-known/did.jsonl. A did:webs community serves no log, so sealing always failed and the console fell back to `cnm`. A did:webvh community on a DID host failed the same way. The community now answers vtc/storage/credentials/recipient/0.1 (trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#1329): - It returns the Ed25519 key it opens sealed blocks with, as a did:key, plus the verification method that publishes it (item 2). - When its own DID resolves, the answer is checked against that document. If the document publishes a different signing key, the answer is `notPublished` (retryable) and carries no key, so nothing is sealed to a key that has rotated away (item 3). - It requires `vtc.rooms.admin`, the same authority as credentials/set (item 1). The console asks this task instead of reading did.jsonl. It accepts the answer only when it names the community's own DID (item 4) and seals to it as given (item 5). - **vtc-service**: Store and serve an uploaded community logo ([#2751](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2751)) * feat(vtc-service): store and serve an uploaded community logo A community can now upload its logo, and the VTC serves it from its own origin, so it shows in the console, the member portal, both sign-in pages and the default landing page wherever the VTC is hosted. Before this, the logo was only the profile's `logoUrl`. Those pages are served with `img-src 'self' data:`, so a logo at any other address was never drawn, and a deployment with nowhere on the VTC's own origin to put a file (a hosted VTC, say) had no logo at all: a filesystem website must have its own host, and `admin_ui.members_dir` is a snapshot that stops following the daemon on every upgrade. What it adds: - `vtc/community/logo/update/0.1` (pinned in `vti-specs-vtc`): an administrator (`vtc.surface.admin`) sends a PNG, JPEG or WebP, or `image: null` to remove the logo. The community re-encodes it as a PNG of at most 512 px (`directory::images::reencode_logo`, sharing the directory's decoding and its bounds), dropping all metadata and any bytes after the image data, and stores it in the `community` keyspace, which is backed up. 20 changes per administrator per hour, one re-encoding at a time, audited as `CommunityLogoUpdated` by digest. - `GET /v1/community/logo`: public, like `public-profile`. Served from memory against a small record read, with a fixed `Content-Type`, `nosniff`, `default-src 'none'; sandbox`, an `ETag` and `304`. Bytes that do not match their record are never served. - A `logo` member (`url`, `sha256`, `mediaType`, `width`, `height`) on the public profile and on `/v1/member/me`'s `community`. Every page draws it in preference to `logoUrl`, which is unchanged. - Console: a Logo card on the Community profile page. It rasterizes an SVG in the browser, from a `data:` URL inside an `` where it runs no script, so no SVG is ever sent or stored. The Logo URL field now says when these pages will not draw the address it holds. Design note: docs/05-design-notes/vtc-community-logo.md.

## `vtc-client`
## [0.45.1](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/compare/vtc-client-v0.45.0...vtc-client-v0.45.1) — 2026-11-18 ### Fixed - **vtc-client**: Send_task keeps a refusal's document over a session ([#2768](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2768)) send_task promised VtcError::Refused over a session, carrying the trust-task-error document, but sent through the typed `document` helper, which asks the session for the payload alone and turns a refusal into a one-line VtcError::Session. A generic caller acts on what that drops: a refusal's details carry the step-up the community asks the person for (stepUpHandoff, VTI-LNK-125 - 131). Seen through vtc-mcp: vtc/rooms/community/create answered "a passkey gesture bound to this operation is required" as a transport error, with no link for the person's wallet, so an administrator with an enrolled approver could not answer the step-up at all. Over a session send_task now asks for the reply document and reads it as the HTTPS path reads one: a trust-task-error is NotFound where it carries one of the task's declared codes saying the thing is absent, else Refused with the document as received; a next-step is Parked; a response is its payload. The typed methods are unchanged.

## `vta-keys`
## [0.44.1](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/compare/vta-keys-v0.44.0...vta-keys-v0.44.1) — 2026-11-18 ### Added - **vta-signing**: A small signing library the VTA and its callers share ([#2745](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2745)) * feat(keys): keys/sign-jws/0.1 — a VTA-built compact JWS walled off to JWT types Add a `keys/sign-jws/0.1` Trust Task that produces a compact JWS (a JWT) over a caller-supplied JOSE header and claims set, signed by a stored key. Two places assumed one signing key per identity: - vault/sign-trust-task signed every document with the entry's one stored signingKeyId. A wallet sign-in signs auth/oob/identify for authentication and auth/oob/grant for assertionMethod, so a community refused one of the two whichever key the entry named (VTI-KEY-022). Where the principal is a key-role did:webs this agent holds, the purpose now decides the key; every other principal still signs with the entry's key. The key is still held to the entry's context (custody rule 7). - vta/dids/list reported the key event log's key as signingKeyId, which a client then stored in the entry: a method the document lists nowhere. It now reports the operational key for a key-role identity. persona_key_for also answers for a key-role did:webs, with the role key of the relationship, checked against the identity's own document and held to the same record checks as a level-1 identity. - **vta-service**: Refuse to sign a document as the did:key of a did:w… ([#2765](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2765)) * fix(vta-service): refuse to sign a document as the did:key of a did:webvh update key A VTA-built did:webvh uses one key as its signing key and its log's update key. keys/sign-document signed a caller's document as the did:key of any key in the caller's scope, so a holder of sign-document in the context could have the update key sign a forged log entry (a proof by did:key: is exactly a log entry's) that adds its own key to the DID, and keep that key after its grant is revoked. sign-document now refuses to sign as a did:key whose key is an active update or pre-rotation key of a did:webvh this VTA holds. The test hosts put the DID in `didUrl`, so no test caught it. `RequestUriResponse` carries the record's `didId` as `did_id`, and both the own-identity publish and create check it. The test hosts answer as a host does: `didUrl` the log's URL, `didId` the identifier. - **vta-service**: A TSP-only VTA boots (#937 follow-up) ([#2743](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2743)) #937 let a VTA speak TSP without DIDComm: setup accepts TSP alone, and the mediator connect supervisor opens for `services.didcomm || services.tsp`. Two places in `server::run` were missed, so a TSP-only VTA set up that way refused to start with "no services enabled — enable at least one of REST or DIDComm": - The pre-loop guard, and the restart loop's warning, counted only REST and DIDComm. Both now ask `any_transport_enabled`, which counts REST, DIDComm or TSP, each built and enabled. WebAuthn alone is still not a transport. - `services.tsp` was migrated into the runtime state on first boot but never mirrored back at boot or on a soft restart, unlike REST and DIDComm, so `pnm services tsp {enable,disable}` did not survive a restart. ## [0.2.1](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/compare/vtc-audit-v0.2.0...vtc-audit-v0.2.1) — 2026-11-18 ### Added - **vtc-service**: Store and serve an uploaded community logo ([#2751](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2751)) * feat(vtc-service): store and serve an uploaded community logo A community can now upload its logo, and the VTC serves it from its own origin, so it shows in the console, the member portal, both sign-in pages and the default landing page wherever the VTC is hosted. The path prompt now follows the chosen method and refuses `.well-known` for a did:webs, as `vtc setup --from` and the VTA do. The hosting intro presents both DID shapes instead of did:webvh alone. title: fix!: verify every VTA reply, and sign the TSP announce
body:
This is the app side of OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1744. It follows two VTI changes:

- #1739: the VTA and the VTC accept a Trust Task over DIDComm or TSP only when its proof verifies as its `issuer`, and that issuer is the transport sender.
- #1740: every VTA and VTC response, errors included, is signed under `proofPurpose: authentication`.

## What the app sends

The app already sent only signed documents built by the engine: `whoami`, step-up approve/deny, task-consent approve/deny and `device/set-wake`, each with a fresh `urn:uuid` id, `issuedAt`, `issuer` set to the device `did:key` and `recipient` set to the VTA. With #1744 the engine:

- signs these under `authentication`, except the approver's own decisions: the step-up `approve-response` and the `task-consent/decision` (approve and deny for each). These are evidence the executor records, so they are signed under `assertionMethod`, and only with a key the device's `did:key` lists there;
- refuses to send any document that is unsigned, or is not issued by this holder to this VTA.

The one unsigned document was the TSP reachability announce, an unsigned `messaging/ping/0.1` that #1739 refuses. It is replaced by `VtaMobileAgent.announceTsp`, which sends a holder-signed ping. The engine's `announce` is removed.

The app sends none of the legacy DIDComm protocol messages that #1739 removes. It uses only the Trust Task envelope over DIDComm and the TSP binding envelope.

## Pushed approval requests

The step-up approve-request, consent request and task-consent request the VTA pushes are its operational messages. #1740 signs them with the operational key under `authentication`, and the #1744 engine refuses one signed under `assertionMethod`, or with a key the issuer does not list under `authentication`, before it prompts. The signed step-up fixtures in `AuthorizationContextTests` are re-signed under `authentication` with the same deterministic test key (seed 17). They were re-signed and checked with the engine's `verify_signed_request` in a throwaway Rust test.

## How replies are verified

| Transport | Where | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| DIDComm | engine, inside `MediatorSession.sendTrustTask` | proof by the VTA under `authentication` (key listed under `authentication`); `threadId` and `type` answer the request; issued by the VTA to this device |
| TSP | `TspReplyRouter.deliver`, via `verifyTrustTaskReply` | same, checked **before** the waiting `submit` is resolved |

Over TSP, a frame that echoes a `threadId` but fails verification is not consumed. The expectation stays open, so the genuine reply still resolves the submit, and a reply that never verifies times out. Error replies must verify too.

## Also

- Re-vendors `Sources/VtaMobileCore/VtaMobileCore.swift`, generated from the #1744 engine. The diff is large because the generator on main has moved on since the v0.6.17 release was vendored.
- The `Package.swift` pin TODO now points at #1744. Until a `vta-mobile-core-v*` release is cut from #1744 and the tag and checksum here are bumped, a checkout needs the local-xcframework override. **CI on this PR is expected to fail until then**: the v0.6.17 binary does not match the vendored bindings, and it still expects pushed requests under `assertionMethod`. No release is cut as part of this PR.
- The README and doc comments describe proof-bound requests and verified replies instead of intrinsic-sender auth, and the exception for the approver's decisions.

## Verification

No full Xcode is installed on the machine this was prepared on (Command Line Tools only), so `xcodebuild test` on a simulator and the XCTest suite were **not** run. What was run:

- `swiftc -typecheck` of `Sources/VtaMobileCore` and `Sources/VtaMobileAgent` against the regenerated bindings and FFI header (macOS target): clean.
- `App/` type-checked for Mac Catalyst (`arm64-apple-ios16.0-macabi`): clean apart from the `#Preview` macro, whose plugin ships only with Xcode.
- A throwaway macOS executable linking the host build of the #1744 engine, exercising the router and the real verifier. All checks passed:
  - a forged reply is not consumed, and the genuine reply resolves the waiter;
  - an unexpected thread passes through;
  - a reply that never verifies times out;
  - the engine refuses an unsigned reply with `UnverifiedReply`;
  - the default router does not consume an unsigned reply.
- The updated `TspReplyRouterTests`, including three new cases for these rules, and the re-signed `AuthorizationContextTests` fixtures were written but not compiled, since XCTest is unavailable here (`swiftc -parse` only).

Not run: an end-to-end test against a deployed VTA built from #1739 and #1740.

title: fix(scripts): resolve repo paths with fileURLToPath so the checks run on Windows
body:
## What and why

`scripts/validate-ceremonies.mjs` and `scripts/lib/schema-bounds.mjs --baseline` derive the repo root from `new URL(..., import.meta.url).pathname`. On Windows that is `/C:/Users/...`, which node's path functions read as relative to the drive root:

- `validate-ceremonies` stops at `no ceremonies/ceremony.meta.schema.json`;
- `schema-bounds --baseline` fails reading `C:\C:\...\specs`.

Both now use `fileURLToPath`, as `build-registry`, `build-go-bindings` and `build-dart-bindings` already do. Nothing changes on Linux or macOS.

Checked on Windows 11, node 22: `validate-ceremonies` validates the three ceremonies; `schema-bounds --baseline` writes the baseline. Before the change, both fail as above.

## Checklist

- [x] Every commit is DCO signed (`git commit -s`).
- [x] The title is a conventional commit; any `!` is scoped to the package whose API breaks.
- [x] If `specs/` changed: all four libraries are regenerated (`npm run regen`) and committed. (No spec changed.)
- [x] No package version and no `CHANGELOG.md` entry is edited — the Release PR does both.
- [x] `npm run check` passes, and the tests for the code touched were run. (On Windows 11, node 22, `npm run check` now completes, including `validate-ceremonies` and `test-ceremonies` (21/21 invalid definitions rejected), which stopped at the first ceremony before.)

See [CONTRIBUTING.md](../CONTRIBUTING.md) and [docs/DEVELOPMENT.md](../docs/DEVELOPMENT.md).

body:
Bumps [vti-vtn](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure) from 0.8.0 to 0.9.0.
Changelog

Sourced from vti-vtn's changelog.

Changelog

Released versions are recorded below, newest first.

This file is frozen. It records everything released up to the adoption of release-plz in #938.

Current entries live in each published crate's own CHANGELOG.md (vta-sdk/CHANGELOG.md, vti-common/CHANGELOG.md, …), generated from conventional commits when a release is cut. The changelog.d/ fragment directory is gone.

Writing an entry: you don't. Write a conventional-commit PR title and a real commit body — see CONTRIBUTING.md and https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/blob/main/RELEASING.md.

Unreleased

Repository — the changelog convention is signposted, enforced, and current (#935)

No crate versions change. Recorded here because it changes where contributors are told to write changelog entries and what CI does about it — exactly the kind of process change changelog.d/README.md asks for a fragment about.

CHANGELOG.md opened with a ## Unreleased section that stopped at #876, while every entry since — 52 fragments — lived in changelog.d/ with nothing in the file saying so.

Signposting. CHANGELOG.md gains a note above ## Unreleased: unreleased entries live in changelog.d/ until a release is cut, this file lags that directory by design, and reading both is how you see everything pending. Above the heading deliberately — collate-changelog.sh inserts fragments immediately after the ## Unreleased line, so a note underneath would sink below the newest entries on every release. CONTRIBUTING.md's PR checklist asked for "CHANGELOG.md updated for user-facing changes" — the one thing the convention forbids, told to every contributor at the moment they were about to do it; it now asks for a fragment, beside a new Changelog section. README.md names both locations.

Enforcement. scripts/check-changelogs.sh gains two rules, because the convention had been documented in four places and enforced in none — and the cost of ignoring it never lands on the author, it lands on every other open PR as a conflict they did not cause:

  • A fragment a PR adds must name that PR, in its filename and in its ### heading. The heading half is the easy mistake — you write the fragment before the PR exists, guess the next number, and lose the race — and it is the worse one, because a wrong number survives collation and permanently points readers at an unrelated PR. Only files this PR adds are checked; the directory holds every open PR's fragment.

Signposting. CHANGELOG.md gains a note above ## Unreleased: unreleased entries live in changelog.d/ until a release is cut, this file lags that directory by design, and reading both is how you see everything pending. Above the heading deliberately — collate-changelog.sh inserts fragments immediately after the ## Unreleased line, so a note underneath would sink below the newest entries on every release. Enforcement. scripts/check-changelogs.sh gains two rules, because the convention had been documented in four places and enforced in none — and the cost of ignoring it never lands on the author, it lands on every other open PR as a conflict they did not cause:

title: feat(pnm): up to ~20× faster commands on a distant VTA (ssh-style ControlMaster)
body:
> **Draft / WIP** — the feature works and is measured, but see *Not done yet* at the bottom.

## Why

Every `pnm` invocation is a fresh process. Each one re-resolves the VTA and mediator DIDs,
opens a TLS connection per host, authenticates to the mediator and upgrades a WebSocket —
and only then sends the command. None of that survives the process, so the next command
pays for all of it again.

On a local stack that is invisible: a round trip costs microseconds, so the setup is free
and every command looks instant. Against a VTA in another region it is the whole story.

Counted off the reverse proxy's access log, one `pnm acl list` over DIDComm is **12–17 HTTPS
requests**: 6 `did.jsonl` fetches, a mediator challenge and authenticate, a WebSocket
upgrade, an inbox drain, the actual outbound/inbound pair, and several cleanup `DELETE`s.
Because each fresh connection also pays TCP and TLS on top of its request, that is **~23
serialised round trips** — for a command whose useful work is one.

## What it costs today, and with this change

`pnm acl list`, three runs per cell, median. Both arms are the same binary and the same
`docker exec` into one long-lived container, so process startup is in neither number; the
~103 ms exec floor is subtracted. Latency injected with a delaying relay in front of the
stack, so these are propagation delay only — no jitter or loss, which makes them floors.

| RTT | one-shot (`--control-master no`) | multiplexed | removed | **ratio** |
|-----:|-----:|-----:|-----:|-----:|
| 0 ms | 64 ms | 41 ms | 23 ms | **1.6×** |
| 50 ms | 1 378 ms | 107 ms | 1 271 ms | **12.9×** |
| 150 ms | 3 646 ms | 215 ms | 3 431 ms | **17.0×** |
| 300 ms | 6 892 ms | 360 ms | 6 532 ms | **19.1×** |

Both sides are linear in RTT, which is the useful form:

```
one-shot     ≈ 22.8 × RTT
multiplexed  ≈  1.06 × RTT
```

The ratio therefore climbs with distance and approaches **~21×** (22.8 / 1.06) as the
fixed local cost stops mattering: 19.1× is what was measured at 300 ms, not a ceiling.

A multiplexed command costs **one application round trip** — the same thing a trust ping
measures. So the rule needs no RTT estimate at all: **the multiplexed number is your trust
ping**, and everything above it is setup the one-shot CLI redoes every time.

| your trust ping | multiplexed | one-shot today |
|-----:|-----:|-----:|
| 50 ms | 50 ms | ~1.2 s |
| 150 ms | 150 ms | ~3.5 s |
| 300 ms | 300 ms | ~7.0 s |

At 300 ms RTT a twenty-command script goes from over two minutes to about seven seconds.

### Starting the master is ~free

The first command has no master to talk to, so it starts one and then delegates. That costs
about what running the command directly would have, because the master does the setup the
command needed anyway:

| RTT | first command (starts master) | one-shot |
|-----:|-----:|-----:|
| 0 ms | 168 ms | 64 ms |
| 50 ms | 1 432 ms | 1 378 ms |
| 150 ms | 3 638 ms | 3 646 ms |
| 300 ms | 7 044 ms | 6 892 ms |

Which is why the default can be `auto`: nobody has to think about it, and nobody pays to
find out.

## What this adds

```
--control-master no|auto|yes|ask    (default: auto)
--control-persist no|yes|10m|600    (default: 10m)
--control-path <PATH>               (default: per-VTA socket in a private dir)

pnm sidecar serve | status | stop   (ssh -M / -O check / -O exit)
```

Names and semantics follow `ssh_config(5)` so the behaviour transfers. Rarely typed:
`auto` starts a master on demand, the way nobody types `ssh -M`.

The client hands the master its own stdin/stdout/stderr over `SCM_RIGHTS`, so a delegated
command's output is indistinguishable from a direct one — same terminal, same `isatty`,
same colours, same redirection.

## Why it is safe to default on

A master that is missing, stale, wrong-version or unusable is **never an error**. Every
such path falls back to the ordinary one-shot command, so the worst case is exactly
today's behaviour. Verified by killing a master with `SIGKILL` and running the next
command: the stale socket is detected, unlinked, replaced, and the command succeeds.

## Security

The master holds the only copy of the operator's admin private key in memory and will run
any command handed to it, so the socket is the privilege boundary:

- control directory forced to `0700` and ownership-checked; socket `0600`
- a symlinked or foreign-owned control path is refused, which closes the path-swap race
- **peer uid verified on every connection** (`SO_PEERCRED` / `getpeereid`) rather than
  trusting file permissions alone, with no exemption for root
- protocol version checked, so a master left running across an upgrade is refused rather
  than guessed at
- `--control-persist 10m` bounds how long the key stays resident — a security control, not
  just resource hygiene
- `ask` confirms before a master is used or created

## Two details taken from the OpenSSH implementation, not its documentation

1. **The socket is claimed atomically.** Binding a temp path and `link()`ing it into place
   means a second master loses with `EEXIST`. The obvious `unlink()`-then-`bind()` would
   remove a live master's socket, leaving that master running but unreachable while every
   later client silently started another. There is a regression test for this.
2. **Stale sockets are removed by the client, on `ECONNREFUSED` only**, and not at all when
   multiplexing is disabled.

Deliberate divergences from ssh are documented in `control/client.rs`: we spawn a child
rather than forking a thread-bearing tokio process; we confirm on the client's terminal so
`ask` works headless (ssh's askpass silently denies with no `DISPLAY`); we vet the control
path, which ssh does not; we do not exempt root from the peer check; and `yes` means "never
silently fall back" rather than ssh's "be the master".

No OpenSSH code is used — the design is reimplemented in Rust.

## Testing

`cargo test -p pnm-cli` — 104 pass, including the socket race, socket mode, path
sanitisation, symlink refusal and the `ControlPersist` time vocabulary. `clippy` and `fmt`
clean.

Against a live stack: idle timeout evicts the master, `sidecar stop` exits it, a
`SIGKILL`ed master is recovered from, `--control-master no` still runs direct, and the
control socket is `0600` inside a `0700` directory on both macOS and Linux.

## Not done yet

- [ ] `-O stop` (stop-listening) as distinct from `-O exit` — matters less here, where a
      session is one short command rather than a shell
- [ ] config-file keys to match the flags, so a default can be set per VTA
- [ ] review of whether `auto` should be the shipped default or opt-in for a release or two
- [ ] the `ask` prompt is per master, not per command — worth deciding which is wanted

body:
Bumps [trust-tasks-rs](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf) from 0.37.5 to 0.37.12.
Release notes

Sourced from trust-tasks-rs's releases.

trust-tasks-rs-v0.37.12

Added

  • messaging/mux: DID multiplexing at a mediator (messaging/mux/*/0.1) (#1068)

  • feat(messaging/mux): DID multiplexing at a mediator (messaging/mux/*/0.1)

    One authenticated connection (the principal) carries live delivery and pickup for many member DIDs: session attaches bound to one connection's sessionId/muxNonce, and stored grants a member DID signs once. Members sign closed statements (muxAttach, muxGrant, muxRevokeAll) with an embedded Data Integrity proof (proofPurpose authentication), verified in a normative order before any state changes.

    Adds attach, detach, grant, list, update (narrow only), revoke, revoke-all (epoch advance), event (live: ready/attached/detached/refused, incl. the tsp-mux subprotocol) and notice (durable: grantsSuspended, grantsRevoked, grantsExpiring, grantsPresent), with shared definitions in messaging/mux/_shared/0.1/mux.schema.json, stable per-statement refusal codes, the unknown-key suspension rule and replay floors.

    Allowlists eddsa-rdfc-2022 as W3C Data Integrity vocabulary for the casing lint.

  • vta/memory: Versioned writes, tombstones, a change feed and named reads (put/delete/list 0.2, get 0.1) (#1067)

vta/memory 0.1 is an unconditional upsert key/value store: put overwrites with no version, so two writers clobber each other undetected; delete is a hard delete, so another device's cached copy never learns the item is gone; and list returns the whole context with no prefix, paging or change feed.

The new versions apply vta/app-state's semantics to memory, restated per spec so each can be implemented on its own:

  • A per-context write counter (MemoryRecord.version, in the new shared definition vta/_shared/0.1/memory-record) serves both as the optimistic-concurrency token and the sync watermark.
  • put/0.2: optional expectedVersion (0 = create only). A failed precondition is versionConflict, with the current version and value in its details so the loser need not re-read. The response returns version, wasCreated, updatedAt and valueBytes. valueTooLarge carries limitBytes / actualBytes. currentValue is withheld from a caller that may write the context but not read it.
  • delete/0.2: leaves a tombstone, takes an optional positive expectedVersion, and treats deleting nothing as success (existed: false).
  • list/0.2: a snapshot (prefix, cursor/limit, values by default as in 0.1) or a change feed from sinceVersion that includes tombstones, with highWatermark, watermarkTooOld and cursorInvalid.
  • get/0.1 (new): up to 256 named keys, each answered once in items,

... (truncated)

title: fix(vtc-client): send_task keeps a refusal's document over a session
body:
## Problem

Through `vtc-mcp`, an operation that needs the person's own step-up could not be answered. `vtc/rooms/community/create` came back as

```
session transport error: forbidden: a passkey gesture bound to this operation is required
```

with no step-up link, although the administrator held an enrolled approver and the community had minted a hand-off (VTI-LNK-125 – 131).

`VtcClient::send_task` documents `VtcError::Refused` over a session, carrying the `trust-task-error` document. It sent through the typed `document` helper, which asks the session for the payload alone and maps a refusal to `VtcError::Session(String)`. The refusal's `details`, including `stepUpHandoff`, were dropped before `vtc-mcp` could build the link. Only the `acl` and `git-ns` paths, which use `dispatch_trust_task_document`, kept it.

## Change

Over a session, `send_task` asks for the reply document and reads it as the HTTPS path reads one:

- a `trust-task-error` is `NotFound` where it carries one of the task's declared codes saying the thing is absent, else `Refused` with the document as received;
- a `trust-task-next-step` is `Parked`;
- a `#response` is its payload.

The typed methods and the HTTPS path are unchanged.

## Testing

- New: `a_session_refusal_keeps_its_document_and_the_step_up_it_carries`, `a_session_reply_is_read_as_the_https_one_is`.
- `cargo test -p vtc-client --features didcomm --lib send::` (10 passed), `cargo test -p vtc-mcp`, and clippy on both with `-D warnings`.
- End to end against a live community over TSP: the same `vtc/rooms/community/create` call now answers `stepUpRequired` with a link; after the wallet approved it, the identical call created the room.
- Not run: the full workspace suite.

title: Automated vetting run: peer and hidden vetting pass end to end, unattended
body:
## Summary

`infra/scripts/vetting-run.sh all` now runs peer vetting, then hidden (PCS) vetting, end to end against the local Docker stack. There is no human in the loop.

**People and services:**
- Four real OpenVTC clients:
  - two vetters, `carol` and `dave`
  - one applicant per flow: `alice-<run>` for peer vetting, `bob-<run>` for hidden vetting
- One real mediator, DID host, VTA and VTC.

**How it is driven:**
- Each client is the production `openvtc` (state handler, VTA session, mediator listeners, inbound handling). `openvtc script …` drives it in place of the TUI. That mode is behind the off-by-default feature `scripted`, in `openvtc/openvtc/src/script_cmd*`.
- The administrator's console steps are scripted with a virtual WebAuthn passkey over the Chrome DevTools Protocol (`infra/bin/console`; no npm packages).

## Verified

Final unattended run: `vetting-run.sh all`, exit 0. The VTC logs show:

- **Peer:** `join request decided under criterion criterion=kernel-developer`. The applicant presented two named Vetting Statements.
- **Hidden:** `hidden-vetting proof verified and counted … criterion=kernel-developer-hidden attestations=2 counted=2`, then `verdict="allow"`. The community counts two distinct vetters without learning who they are.

Tests:
- `openvtc-core`: 1,224 lib tests pass.
- `openvtc`: 1,418 tests pass.
- `cargo check --all-targets` is clean with and without `scripted`.

## Fixes found on the way

These all block any OpenVTC client against a `localhost` stack. Each applies only under `VTA_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ENDPOINTS`; without it, behaviour is unchanged.

- **Runtime TDK:** the state handler's own TDK resolved with the public-only host policy, so join-status polls could not be packed.
- **Status list:** the client refused a membership credential whose revocation status list is served over http.
- **Manifest:** the client refused to read the community's manifest over http.
- **Mediator:** its Trust Task proof verifier refused the VTC's delivery-status checks. Fixed with a local patch on the same `MEDIATOR_ALLOW_PRIVATE_DID_HOSTS` opt-in. The image now builds in an 8 GB Docker VM.

## Notes for reviewers

- A vetter's client treats a community that hides *any* criterion's vetters as hiding all of them. So the run does named vetting with no hidden criterion present, then adds `kernel-developer-hidden` and turns hidden vetting on.
- The vetters' own admission (`console approve-join`) and their vetter grant (`cnm vetting vetters grant`) are done by the script as the administrator.

All commits are signed, with DCO sign-off.

title: feat!: move to pcreds with Jali 0.3.0 and application contexts
body:
Brings the crate up to the research implementation at
[etairi/predicate-credential-system@5d11dc4](https://github.com/etairi/predicate-credential-system/commit/5d11dc4)
with this repository's adjustments, adds application contexts to its protocol for OpenVTC, and
ports the demo to it. It is breaking (`feat!`), so release-plz will propose 0.2.0.

138 files changed (+45,637 / −28,032), of which the demo is 10 files (+901 / −520).

## The library: `pcreds` replaces `pcs` and `cred`

- **`pcreds`** is the protocol `Π_PCreds` of the paper's revised version, generic over its
  building blocks (`pcreds::Backend`). The modules `pcs` and `cred` are removed.
- **Pairing instantiations:** `Σ-PS` and `Σ-BBS` with `Tag_DDH` and `Tag_DY` over BLS12-381. The
  sigma protocols follow `draft-irtf-cfrg-sigma-protocols-04` and
  `draft-irtf-cfrg-fiat-shamir-04` (SHAKE128 duplex sponge), with the drafts' vectors in
  `kat/ietf/`.
- **Lattice instantiation** (feature `lattice`): `Σ-vSIS` on an NTRU trapdoor with `Tag_LWR`,
  proved with [Jali](https://crates.io/crates/jali) 0.3.0 and `ntru-trapdoor` 0.1.1, both from
  crates.io and pinned exactly. Its proofs are straight-line extractable by default (Katsumata's
  transform). The feature `lattice-plain` selects plain Fiat–Shamir, and the two builds refuse
  each other's parameters and proofs. `lattice-extractable` stays as an alias.
- **Unchanged:** edition 2024, `rust-version = "1.95.0"`, MIT, no default features,
  `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`.

## Application contexts (for OpenVTC, not in the paper)

| Party | Binds | Checked with |
|---|---|---|
| Attester | `attest_in_context(.., app)`: `π_att` bound to `app` | `check_attestation_in_context(hvk, id_q, att, app)` |
| Requester | `request_credential_in_context(.., att_apps, ssid, app)`: `π_iss` bound to each attestation's context, in order, and to the request's own `app` | `evaluate_request_in_context(helper, request, ssid, att_apps, app)` |

- Without contexts, every context is the paper's byte for byte, and the known answers are
  unchanged. An empty context is not the same as none.
- Verifiers take the context bytes from their own copy of the public data.
- Tags do not depend on contexts, so one attester counts once for a recipient whatever contexts
  its attestations carry.
- Documented in `docs/design-notes.md` ("Contexts") and `docs/encodings.md`, and tested in
  `tests/application_context.rs` (6 tests, `Σ-PS` and `Σ-BBS`).

## The demo on `pcreds`

`demo/README.md` ("Changes for `pcreds`") has the details. In short:

- **Vetter periods become helper keys.** `pcreds` has no class labels, and identifiers and
  tags are functions of the helper key (`x_0 = H_id(⟨hvk⟩)`, `x_Q = H_req(⟨pp, hvk, id_Q, j_Q⟩)`).
  So the class labels `vetter/<period>` of design §13 C1 become one helper key per period, the
  epoch rotation of §4.3.
  - *Kept:* removal stays cryptographic. A removed vetter gets no credential under the next
    period and cannot attest at all once its last period is dropped. The window of two live
    periods stays, and one vetter still counts once per request.
  - *Given up:* one request can no longer mix periods, which was C1's aim. An application in
    flight completes under its period while that period is live. After the period is dropped,
    the applicant registers again and the vetters refresh their statements without a new
    session, with new tags. Vetters enrol with a fresh key per period (§18.2), so C2's lifelong
    identifier becomes one identifier per member and period.
  - *Considered and not taken:* one long-lived helper key with the period carried only by the
    token labels. It would keep mixing, but a removed vetter's credential would then stay valid
    for good. Removal would rest on token scarcity alone, and a current vetter could hand tokens
    to a removed one so that it counts as a second, distinct vetter.
- **Tokens use one `Σ-PS` key per label.** The `Σ-PS` of `pcreds` signs one scalar, the serial,
  so the label is in the key (the per-month token keys of §5.1).
- **The submission is a `pcreds` credential request** under `ssid = challenge`, bound to every
  statement's metadata and to the proof context. The VTC evaluates it (`N''`) and never answers
  it with a credential. Its helpers use a policy no request meets, so every credential under a
  period's key is a root admission (C4). A statement whose attestation does not verify is now
  `unverified` and simply does not count. Before, one invalid attestation failed the whole proof.
- **Tests:** 14 end-to-end tests, with VTI's own `requirements::evaluate`. Mutation check: each
  of eight VTC defences was disabled in turn, and each time the test that covers it failed.

## CI

- Clippy runs with `--all-features` (the extractable lattice build) and with the plain set.
- Tests run with `--all-features --all-targets` and with `--features lattice-plain`.
- Docs build in both lattice modes with `-D warnings`, and docs.rs gets `serde, jali, lattice`.
- A new `lattice` job runs `quick_end_to_end_k1` and `proofs_are_in_the_mode_of_the_build` in
  release, in both modes, with the same pinned actions.
- Format, no-default-features, MSRV and package are unchanged. The demo is still not built in
  CI.

## Lockfile

- New: `jali` 0.3.0 and `ntru-trapdoor` 0.1.1, with Jali's dependencies `aes` 0.9.4, `cipher`
  0.5.2, `crypto-primes` 0.7.2, `ctr` 0.10.1 and `inout` 0.2.6.
- Upgraded, and shared with the demo's tree: `crypto-bigint` 0.7.5 → 0.7.11 and `ctutils`
  0.4.2 → 0.4.8.
- The demo's pins (`vta-sdk =0.56.1`) and the rest of its tree are unchanged.

## Kept from `main`

- `Cargo.toml`: the MSRV comment, the author note (now naming base commit 5d11dc4),
  `repository`, publishing (no `publish = false`) and `[workspace] members = ["demo"]`.
- `README.md`: the demo link, and the sentence on the crates.io release by release-plz.
- `release-plz.toml`, `RELEASING.md`, `LICENSE` and `publish.yml` are untouched.
- `docs/openvtc-integration.md` comes from the research repository, corrected where its text is
  wrong for this one (the crate is published, and attestations can carry an application
  context), and without the research repository's outdated note on the extraction of the
  proofs.

## Consumers and related work

- VTI's workspace depends on `predicate-credential-system = "0.1"`, so `vti-vetting-pcs`, which
  uses the class labels of `pcs`, stays on 0.1.x until it is ported. That port is the same one
  the demo went through here.
- This supersedes the `post-quantum` branch (two commits on `main`, no PR), which added a
  lattice instantiation to the old API. It can be deleted once this merges.
- #4 (interactive walkthrough) changes the same demo files on the old API, so it needs a port to
  this one after this merges.

## Verification

Run locally on 2026-11-16 (macOS arm64, rustc 1.100.0, the toolchain 1.95.0 for MSRV), on this
tree before it was committed:

title: feat(vtc-service)!: serve the landing page from a directory (website.landing_dir)
body:
## Why

A community wanting its own landing page had to either edit `vtc-service/website-default/` and rebuild the daemon, or set `website.root_dir` — which must sit on a separate host, because administrators can deploy into it over the network and it would otherwise ride the console's session cookie.

## What

`[website] landing_dir = "<dir>"`: an operator-placed directory served at the website mount in place of the built-in page, **re-read on every request** — edits show on the next load, no rebuild, no restart, no second host.

- **Same-origin is safe here**: nothing over the network writes it (`/v1/website/*` deploy/file tasks act only on `root_dir`), so it carries the operator's trust — the footing `admin_ui.dir` / `members_dir` already have.
- **Boot check** (fails closed): readable `index.html`, directory and `index.html` not world-writable. The check is now shared with the console/portal directories as `website::paths::check_operator_dir`.
- `root_dir` + `landing_dir` together is refused at config load.
- Paths go through the website safety chain (`canonical_within_root`: no hidden files, no escape incl. symlinks, no exec bit); misses and directory requests fall back to `index.html` as HTML; `Cache-Control: no-cache`; default CSP still applies.
- `vtc website export <dir>` writes the built-in page out as a starting point (refuses a non-empty directory).

## Breaking

- `WebsiteConfig` gains `landing_dir`.
- `routes::router_with` / `router_with_xff` / `assemble_with_website` take `website::WebsiteSource` (`BuiltIn | Landing(PathBuf) | Filesystem(WebsiteState)`) instead of `Option<WebsiteState>`.

## Tests

- Unit: export round-trip + serve from disk + edit picked up; nothing outside the directory / no hidden file served; boot check (missing index, world-writable); config exclusivity and path-mode acceptance.
- Integration: `routing_modes::path_mode_serves_the_landing_dir_beside_the_other_surfaces` — `/` serves the directory, `/health` and `/admin/` keep their surfaces, an edit shows on the next request.
- `cargo nextest run -p vtc-service -p vtc-client`: 3796 passed. `cargo clippy -p vtc-service --all-targets -- -D warnings` clean. `scripts/check-docs.py` passes.

## Docs

`docs/03-vtc/website-and-admin.md` (*Your own landing page, from a directory*, config block, quick reference, path-mode note), `docs/03-vtc/getting-started.md` step 6, `vtc-service/website-default/README.md`.

title: fix(vta-service)!: a key-role did:webs signs with the key of the proof's purpose
body:
## Problem

A wallet sign-in to a community as a key-role `did:webs` identity is always refused.

A key-role did:webs publishes a different key for each relationship (VTI-KEY-072): its `operational` key under `authentication`, its `attestation` key under `assertionMethod`, and the key event log's own key under neither. A sign-in signs two documents: `auth/oob/identify` for `authentication` and `auth/oob/grant` for `assertionMethod`.

- `vault/sign-trust-task` signed every document with the vault entry's one stored `signingKeyId`, so the community refused one of the two steps whichever key the entry named (VTI-KEY-022). Seen against a live VTC as `carried document proof does not verify` at `prove`, then, with the authentication key entered by hand, `verificationMethod is not listed under assertionMethod in its DID document` at `respond`.
- `vta/dids/list` reported the key event log's key as `signingKeyId`. The browser wallet stores that value in the entry, so the default entry named a method the document lists nowhere.

## Change

- `operations::persona`: `persona_key_for` answers for a key-role did:webs with the role key of the relationship, checked against the identity's own document and held to the same record checks as a level-1 identity. New `role_key_id_for` names that key record where the identity, not the caller, decides the key.
- `operations::vault::sign_trust_task::sign_envelope`: where the principal is a key-role did:webs this agent holds, the proof purpose decides the key. Every other principal still signs with the entry's key. The key is still held to the entry's context (custody rule 7).
- `operations::dids`: the listing reports the `operational` key as `signingKeyId` for a key-role did:webs.

## Breaking

`sign_envelope` takes the persona stores (`PersonaStores`), a signature change in a published crate.

## Testing

- New: `a_key_role_did_webs_is_a_persona_signing_with_the_key_of_the_relationship`, `a_did_webs_without_key_roles_names_no_role_key`.
- Ran `cargo test -p vta-service --lib` filtered to the did:webs persona, DID listing and vault tests: 68 passed.
- Not run: the full workspace suite. Not yet tried end to end against the VTA and VTC where the failure was seen.

## Not in this PR

- The level a key-role identity reports in `vta/dids/list` is still `1`.
- The legacy SIOP `proxy-login` path still uses the entry's stored key.

title: fix(onboarding): reach a did:webs agent's REST endpoint
body:
Onboarding asked `didWebvhDomain` which host to request access to. For a did:webs agent that returns `undefined`, so the wallet asked for no grant, and its first REST call was refused by the browser as CORS with nothing to say why. vta-service's REST layer is origin-allowlisted, so the extension must hold the host permission.

There are two causes, and this fixes both.

1. **The method.** New core `didHost(did)` returns the host a DID names whatever its method: did:webvh, did:webs (first segment), or a did:scid's `src`. A DID that names no host (did:key, did:peer, a bare did:scid) returns nothing. Onboarding's up-front grant and its resume-after-the-permission-dialog path both use it.
2. **The host.** An agent's REST endpoint is not always on its DID's host. A did:webs is published on a shared hosting server, so for one it never is. Once `prepare` has read the agent's document, the view checks the REST base URL's origin. If that origin isn't granted, it shows **Allow access to <host>** on its own click, because the first click's user gesture is spent by then.
   - **Beside a relay** (TSP or DIDComm): the grant is optional, and Connect isn't held back, since REST is then only the fallback.
   - **REST is the only transport:** the grant is required, and Connect stays disabled until it lands, rather than failing as an unexplained CORS refusal.

The setup pane's *agent reachable* check now reads the connection's `restBaseUrl`, which is what the wallet actually fetches, and falls back to the DID's host.

## Tests

- **core** `did.host.mjs`: host per method, a port kept encoded, and no host for did:key, did:peer, a bare did:scid or a did:webs with no AID.
- **render** `onboard-scope`:
  - a did:webs agent's host is requested;
  - a REST origin on another host is offered beside a relay;
  - with REST as the only transport, Connect is held back until the origin is allowed.

`npm test` and `npm run build` pass.

title: fix(vta-service): refuse to sign a document as the did:key of a did:w…
body:
Title
fix(vta-service): refuse to sign a document as the did:key of a did:webvh update key

Body
## What and why

A `did:webvh` the VTA builds uses one key twice: as the DID's signing key and as
the update key that authorizes the DID's log. `keys/sign-document` signed a
caller's document as the `did:key` of any key in the caller's scope, including
that one. A proof by `did:key:<update key>` is exactly what a log entry carries.
So any holder of `sign-document` in the context could have the VTA sign a forged
log entry that adds the caller's own key to the DID. The caller would then
control the DID, and keep that control after its grant is revoked.

`sign-document` now refuses to sign as a `did:key` whose key is an active update
key or pre-rotation key of a `did:webvh` this VTA holds, and answers `Forbidden`.
The same key still signs as the `did:webvh` it serves, whose proofs name that
DID's own verification method, so legitimate signing is unchanged.

- `did_webvh/webvh_keys.rs`: `is_log_authorization_key` tells whether a public
  key is an `UpdateKey` or `PreRotation` key of a held `did:webvh`.
- `keys/sign.rs`: `sign_document` checks it before signing as a `did:key`
  (behind the `webvh` feature).
- `docs/02-vta/integration-guide.md` documents the refusal.

**Tests.**

- `only_update_and_pre_rotation_keys_authorize_log_entries`: only those two
  roles count.
- `an_update_key_does_not_sign_as_its_own_did_key`: the refusal.
- `a_forged_log_entry_is_not_signed_by_the_update_key`: the attack, end to end.
- `an_update_key_still_signs_as_the_did_webvh_it_serves`: the legitimate path
  still works.
- `vta-service` nextest: <N> passed; `cargo fmt` and
  `cargo clippy -p vta-service --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings` are
  clean.

## Requirements

None.

## Backport

none (`keys/sign-document` is not in `release/eucalyptus`)

## Checklist

- [x] Targets `main` (or is a backport / `release-direct` PR into `release/<name>`)
- [x] No `version =` edits in any `Cargo.toml`
- [x] Tests cover the change; `cargo fmt` and `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` are clean

title: fix(vta-service): refuse to sign a document as the did:key of a did:w… (#2765)
body:
fix(vta-service): refuse to sign a document as the did:key of a did:w… (#2765)

* fix(vta-service): refuse to sign a document as the did:key of a did:webvh update key

A VTA-built did:webvh uses one key as its signing key and its log's update
key. keys/sign-document signed a caller's document as the did:key of any key in
the caller's scope, so a holder of sign-document in the context could have the
update key sign a forged log entry (a proof by did:key:<update key> is exactly a
log entry's) that adds its own key to the DID, and keep that key after its grant
is revoked.

sign-document now refuses to sign as a did:key whose key is an active update or
pre-rotation key of a did:webvh this VTA holds. The key still signs as the
did:webvh it serves, whose proofs name that DID's own method.

Signed-off-by: Denys Popov <denys.p@affinidi.com>

* fix(vta-service): read log authority from the did:webvh logs, not the key-handle index

The guard asked the webvh key-handle index whether a key authorizes a
log. That index is bookkeeping, and three of its gaps let a forged entry
through:
- After an update that declares no keys, the previous version's handles
  are superseded and nothing is reinstalled, while the update key stays
  in force.
- DIDs created before the index existed have no handles.
- An update key that is also a verification method is filed under `vm:`.

`did_webvh::log_authority::log_authorized_by` now reads what a verifier
reads. A key is log-authorizing if any entry of a held log names it in
`updateKeys` or commits to its hash in `nextKeyHashes`. Any entry counts,
not only the head, because a proof by an earlier key forks the log. Logs
that do not contain the key or its hash are skipped without parsing. An
unreadable entry fails closed for that DID only, so one bad record
cannot fail every did:key `sign-document` call.

The refusal is `keys/sign-document/0.1` item 6 (a key bound to another
protocol), so it answers `failedPrecondition`, not a bare Forbidden. It
is audited as a key-custody refusal and logged with
`security_alert = true`. The key doubling as update key and verification
method is the VTI-KEY-093 divergence already in the register.

Tests: a metadata-only update, a pre-rotation commitment, and a key the
log lists only as a method (which still signs). The forged-entry test
now asserts the refusal's reason.

title: fix(pcreds): separate empty and absent attestation contexts in π_iss
body:
fix(pcreds): separate empty and absent attestation contexts in π_iss

issuance_context_in appended nothing for att_apps = Some(&[]), the same as
for None, so with no attestations a π_iss proved without application
contexts verified under the context API with an empty att_apps, against the
documented rule that an empty context is not the same as none.

When att_apps is Some, an item att-apps (the number of contexts) now goes
before the att-app items, so Some is distinct from None whatever it holds.
The None encoding is unchanged, so the paper's contexts and the pinned
regression vectors stay as they were. A test covers the zero-attestation
case and fails without the fix.

title: fix(demo): address review findings on the pcreds port
body:
fix(demo): address review findings on the pcreds port

- vtc: issue_vetter_root rebuilds the enrolment ssid for the submitting
  member instead of taking it from the caller, so a captured root request
  cannot be replayed by another member to lock its owner out of the period
- vtc: refuse a request with more than MAX_ATTESTATIONS (64) attestations
  before any pairing check (the period policy's k = usize::MAX rules out
  Policy::with_max_attestations)
- vtc: run the requirements-digest and expiry checks before the token
  checks, so an ineligible statement does not burn its token
- vtc: rotate refuses a period name that is already live
- vetter: attest signs before it spends the reserved token, so a failed
  attestation (e.g. in refresh) leaves the token reserved and release()
  returns it, instead of losing it
- vetter: drop the plain usk copy in Enrolment and use User::expose_key,
  so the per-period key is only held where it is wiped on drop
- applicant: replace checks the new attestation before dropping the old one
- ci: the self dev-dependency comment now lists jali and lattice too

Regression tests for the replay, rotate, attestation limit, token-burn and
replace fixes.

title: fix(links): a did:webs community can issue a sign-in link
body:
Reported live: a sign-in link from the SEDI VTC, whose DID is `did:webs:webvh.storm.ws:sedi-vtc:…`, opened the wallet's *Update needed — This code needs a newer version of the app.*

That message is VTI-LNK-021's `update` outcome. It is what a reader must say for a contact DID method it has no resolver for (`unsupported-vid`), and the wallet's contact-method table listed did:webvh, did:web and did:scid only. A test even pinned `did:webs:example.org` as unsupported.

The spec covers did:webs:
- **VTI-LNK-119** names it as a route-A, host-named contact.
- **VTI-LNK-052** has the reader verify its KERI key event log.

`@openvtc/vti-didcomm-js` 0.16 already does this: it verifies every event, signature, pre-rotation commitment and designation, and builds the document from that state, never from `did.json` alone.

## Changes

- **`WEBS_CONTACT_POLICY`**: route A. Well-formed means a host and an AID. The person is shown the host and path, not the AID (`webvh.storm.ws/sedi-vtc`).
- **`WEBS_CONTACT_METHOD`**: runs the existing `assertResolvableWebsHost` egress check first, then the resolver. The document must carry the DID's own id.

## Tests (`did.contact-methods.mjs`, `links.trigger-link.mjs`)

- Acceptance, route and label.
- Resolution, and a document for another id refused.
- A key event log that does not verify → `did-document-unverified`.
- A `localhost%3A8000` host refused before anything is fetched.
- A did:webs with no AID → `bad-from`.

`npm test` and `npm run build` pass.

A SEDI VTC whose DID is a did:webs issued a sign-in link and the wallet

stream and builds the document from it, never from did.json alone. So:

- WEBS_CONTACT_POLICY: route A; well-formed with a host and an AID; the
  host and path (not the AID) are what the person is shown.
- WEBS_CONTACT_METHOD: the existing assertResolvableWebsHost egress check,
  then the resolver; the document is held to the DID's own id.

Tests pin acceptance, route and label, resolution, a log that does not
verify, the host rules (localhost refused before anything is fetched), and
